newsitem.title: POLAND: POLISH PEASANTS AT CROSSROADS BEFORE CONVENTION.
newsitem.headline: POLISH PEASANTS AT CROSSROADS BEFORE CONVENTION.

text.p: Poland's co-ruling Peasant Party begins a convention on Friday which analysts say will help shape key national policies until the end of the century, including the pace of reforms and integration with the West.

The Polish Peasant Party (PSL), now in an uneasy coalition with a larger ex-communist party but likely to be part of any future cabinet after elections due late next year, will choose its leader and set a new programme at the two-day event.
The leadership contest is set to pit current party chief Waldemar Pawlak against Agriculture Minister Roman Jagielinski. Some other candidates may also stand.

Western diplomats said a victory for Jagielinski, a 49-year-old major landowner with economically more liberal policies, would better serve Poland's drive for European Union entry than would the re-election of Pawlak, 37.

As the coalition's prime minister until early last year, Pawlak was accused by critics, inside and out of the coalition led by the ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD), of braking market reforms and notably privatisation policy.

"Minister Jagielinski has a full grasp of European integration issues and of the difficulties that need to be overcome and tackled," a senior Western diplomat, who asked not to be named, told Reuters.
"Mr Pawlak also knows what European integration is about but some of his public statements on this and on economic policies give rise to some question marks," the diplomat added.

Pawlak and his supporters, representing hosts of small, poorer farmers often worried over EU entry, have attacked sales of state assets and land to foreigners and repeatedly call for protection of domestic farms against international competition.

The Peasants shared power under the communist system toppled in 1989, but have shifted to the right and now share many of the Roman Catholic, sometimes economically populist values of the main opposition grouped around the Solidarity trade union.

Public opinion polls have shown for many months that the Peasants, backed by around 15 percent of voters, are likely to hold the balance of power in the next parliament, with the SLD and the opposition both winning between 20 and 30 percent.
Both the main candidates for Peasant leadership say that should the Solidarity-rooted opposition snatch a substantial vote next year they could form a government with it.

This is why, analysts say, it is so important who will become their leader for the next four years, when Poland will be negotiating its European Union membership, a process that the community says could start early in 1998.

"Not much will change short term -- no matter who becomes leader, the Peasants will stay in the coalition until general elections and then will keep options open for a new one," political analist Stefan Bratkowski said.

Pawlak, a shrewd backstage politician, remains popular among many farmers as the man who led the Peasants to a strong showing in the 1993 elections and whose policies allowed many of the party's members to gain government posts.
Analysts say that if Pawlak loses, support for the Peasants might initially drop but then could then grow as new policies attract supporters from outside the party's agrarian base.
"Other leader,...such as Jagielinski, could attract new electorates to the Peasants," said Halina Franczak, a sociologist at the Demoskop polling agency.
